tools: Tool calling and agents.
On its own, a language model can only write text.
Tool calling changes that.
The tool you're using tells the model which tools exist, such as
read a file, run a command, or search the web.
When the model decides it needs one, it writes a short, structured
request instead of a normal reply.
The app runs that tool for real, and sends the result back
to the model.
The model reads the result, and decides what to do next: call
another tool, or give its answer.
Put that in a loop, and you have an agent.

training: How models are trained.
A model is built in stages.
First comes pre-training.
The model reads trillions of tokens of text and code, and learns
to predict the next token.
This is where its knowledge comes from, and it's by far the
most expensive step.
The result is powerful, but it isn't yet a helpful assistant.
So next comes fine-tuning: training on examples of good conversations, so
the model learns to follow instructions and answer clearly.
Finally, reinforcement learning.
The model tries tasks, and its answers are scored, by people, by
other models, or by automatic checks like
whether the code passes its tests.
Good answers are rewarded, and the model gradually gets better at what
we actually want.
That last step is a big part of why coding models have
improved so fast.
Click through each stage on this page to see what goes in,
and what comes out.
